Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Systems, Embodiments, Syntax

outputs.L1: Systems and methods are disclosed for extending a programming language with a set of extensions using a strict meta-model. In various embodiments, a set of interfaces is provided to enable synthesis of a schema. Syntax is introduced into an existing programming language to permit construction of schematized data objects. A schema processor module translates a schema representation into new keywords, and a document generator module receives the set of keywords and produces output in a selected form. When code comprising the keyword extensions is parsed, data structure nodes represent keyword actions as a set of functions and implement those function calls with the original metadata. A keyword definition comprises a name, an action to be taken at parse time, and an action to be taken at runtime. The default action at parse time is to inject a function call into the code, and the default action at runtime is to call the function.
outputs.L2:
Disclosed are systems and techniques for augmenting a programming language through a collection of extensions governed by a strict meta-model. In some embodiments, a group of interfaces enables the creation of a schema. New syntax is added to an existing programming language so that schematized data objects can be built.

A schema processor module converts a schema representation into newly defined keywords. A document generator module accepts those keywords and generates output in a chosen format. When source code containing the keyword extensions is parsed, data-structure nodes model the keyword operations as a collection of functions and carry out those function calls using the original metadata.

Each keyword definition includes a name, an operation performed during parsing, and an operation performed during runtime. By default, the parse-time operation inserts a function call into the code, while the runtime operation invokes that function.
outputs.L3:
Systems and methods are disclosed for extending a programming language through the use of language extensions governed by a strict meta-model. The meta-model defines the structure, behavior, and constraints of the extensions, ensuring that new language constructs can be introduced in a consistent and controlled manner. By enforcing a well-defined meta-model, the disclosed approach allows extensions to be added without compromising the integrity, predictability, or compatibility of the underlying programming language.

In some embodiments, interfaces are provided that enable a schema to be synthesized and then used to construct schematized data objects. The schema may describe the organization, attributes, relationships, and permissible values associated with the data objects. Once synthesized, the schema serves as a formal specification for creating, validating, and manipulating data objects that conform to the defined structure. This allows developers or automated tools to generate structured data representations that are both machine-readable and consistent with the language extension framework.

A schema processor module is configured to receive a schema representation and translate that representation into one or more new programming language keywords. The schema representation may be expressed in a declarative format, a structured data format, or another suitable representation. The schema processor analyzes the schema, identifies the constructs to be added to the language, and generates corresponding keyword definitions. These generated keywords extend the programming language by providing syntax and semantics associated with the schema-defined concepts.

A document generator module receives the generated keywords and produces output in a selected form. The selected form may include, for example, source code, documentation, markup, configuration files, intermediate representations, or executable artifacts. By using the generated keywords, the document generator can produce output that reflects the structure and semantics defined by the schema. This enables a consistent workflow in which schemas are transformed into language extensions and then used to generate documents or other artifacts in a desired format.

The keyword definitions may include both parse-time actions and runtime actions. Parse-time actions are performed while source text or input is being parsed and may include validating syntax, constructing internal representations, registering schema elements, or transforming input into an intermediate form. Runtime actions are performed during execution and may include creating objects, invoking behavior, enforcing constraints, or producing generated output. In certain embodiments, default parse-time and runtime actions are provided. These defaults may inject functions into the generated keyword definitions and may cause those functions to be called automatically at appropriate stages. As a result, newly generated keywords can have useful behavior without requiring each keyword definition to be manually implemented from scratch.

Together, these components provide a framework for extending a programming language in a schema-driven manner. A schema can be synthesized, converted into language keywords, and used to construct schematized data objects or generate output in a selected form. The use of strict meta-modeling, modular schema processing, and keyword definitions with parse-time and runtime behavior enables flexible yet disciplined language extension.
outputs.L4:
A programming language can be extended to support strict, meta-model-based keyword extensions that allow new language constructs to be introduced in a controlled and schema-driven manner. In such a system, one or more schemas are synthesized through defined interfaces. These schemas describe the structure, constraints, and expected behavior of new constructs that are to be added to the language. Once a schema has been synthesized, a schema representation can be translated into one or more new keywords or keyword forms that become usable within the source language.

The extended keywords are not arbitrary textual additions. Instead, they are derived from the underlying meta-model and are therefore bound to a well-defined structure. This allows the compiler, interpreter, parser, or related tooling to recognize the new keywords, validate their usage, and associate them with specific data models or operations. As a result, programmers can write code using the new keyword extensions while still benefiting from the syntactic and semantic discipline of the original programming language.

When source code containing the keyword extensions is parsed, the extended constructs may be converted into internal representations. These representations can take the form of function-based data structure nodes, where each node corresponds to an action, operation, or schema-defined object. Such nodes may include information needed during parsing, validation, transformation, execution, or output generation. The nodes can also define parse-time behavior, such as checking whether required fields are present or whether the keyword usage conforms to the schema, as well as runtime behavior, such as constructing objects, invoking functions, or producing serialized data.

The system may also generate documents, code artifacts, configuration files, structured outputs, or other results from the keyword-based representations. Because the keywords are derived from schemas, the generated outputs can be consistent with the meta-model and can preserve the constraints and relationships specified by the schema. This makes it possible to use the original programming language as a host language for constructing schematized data objects, domain-specific structures, or declarative descriptions without requiring a completely separate language.

In this way, the programming language is enhanced with a disciplined extension mechanism. Developers can define schemas through interfaces, translate those schemas into language-level keyword extensions, write source code using the new keywords, and then parse and execute that code to create structured data objects or generate desired outputs. The approach combines the flexibility of extensible language design with the reliability of strict schema validation and meta-model-based representation.
outputs.L5:
Systems, embodiments, and syntax are closely connected concepts in technology, design, and communication.

A **system** is an organized structure made up of different parts that work together to achieve a purpose. Systems can be found in software, machines, organizations, languages, and even natural environments. For example, a computer system includes hardware, software, data, and users, all interacting according to defined rules.

**Embodiments** refer to specific forms or implementations of an idea, invention, or design. In technical writing and patents, an embodiment describes a particular way in which a system or method can be realized. A single concept may have many embodiments, each adapted for different uses, environments, or requirements. For instance, a communication system may be embodied as a mobile application, a web platform, or an embedded device.

**Syntax** is the set of rules that defines how elements are arranged to create meaning or function. In language, syntax controls sentence structure. In programming, syntax determines how code must be written so that a computer can understand and execute it. Within systems, syntax often provides the formal framework that allows components to communicate correctly.

Together, these ideas show how abstract concepts become practical and usable. Systems provide structure, embodiments turn designs into real-world implementations, and syntax ensures that information, instructions, or components are arranged in a valid and meaningful way. Whether in software engineering, legal documentation, or linguistic analysis, understanding systems, embodiments, and syntax is essential for creating clear, reliable, and functional solutions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style abstract for an invention about extending a programming language with schema-driven keyword extensions and a strict meta-model.
counterfactuals.output: A computer-implemented system and method are disclosed for extending a programming language through schema-driven keyword extensions governed by a strict meta-model. The system receives one or more extension schemas defining new language keywords, associated syntactic forms, semantic constraints, type relationships, and permissible transformations. A compiler, interpreter, or language-processing tool validates the extension schemas against a meta-model that specifies allowable extension constructs, dependency rules, namespace behavior, and integration points with a base language grammar and type system. Upon validation, the system incorporates the keyword extensions into parsing, analysis, code generation, tooling, or runtime execution without modifying the core language implementation. The strict meta-model enforces deterministic interpretation, prevents ambiguous syntax, and enables consistent validation, documentation, refactoring, and interoperability among independently developed extensions. In some embodiments, the extensions define domain-specific programming constructs that are translated into base-language constructs or intermediate representations while preserving static analysis and safety guarantees. The invention thereby enables controlled, portable, and verifiable language extensibility.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a software patent describing systems and methods for synthesizing schemas, generating language keywords, and handling parse-time/runtime keyword actions.
counterfactuals.output:
The patent describes techniques for creating and using a language-processing system that can automatically synthesize schemas, generate language keywords, and associate those keywords with actions that occur during parsing or at runtime.

At a high level, the invention covers:

- **Schema synthesis:**  
  The system can generate or derive schemas that define the structure, grammar, or valid forms of a domain-specific language, data format, or programming interface. These schemas may be created from examples, metadata, specifications, user input, or existing code/data structures.

- **Keyword generation:**  
  Based on the synthesized schema, the system can automatically create or select keywords for a language. These keywords may represent commands, data types, operations, configuration options, or other semantic elements of the language.

- **Parse-time actions:**  
  The system can associate certain keywords with actions that are triggered while the language input is being parsed. For example, when a parser encounters a keyword, it may validate syntax, update a parse tree, infer types, enforce constraints, or transform the input into an intermediate representation.

- **Runtime actions:**  
  Keywords may also be linked to behaviors that execute after parsing, during program or workflow execution. These actions can include invoking functions, manipulating data, configuring system behavior, executing commands, or interacting with external services.

- **Separation of syntax and behavior:**  
  The patent appears to emphasize a framework where language syntax, keyword definitions, and keyword-triggered behaviors can be generated, modified, or extended systematically rather than hard-coded manually.

- **Domain-specific language support:**  
  A likely use case is simplifying the creation of domain-specific languages by automatically producing the schema and operational semantics needed for parsing and execution.

- **Extensibility and automation:**  
  The invention aims to reduce manual language-design effort by allowing schemas, keywords, and associated behaviors to be synthesized and bound dynamically or semi-automatically.

In short, the patent concerns a framework for automatically constructing language definitions and connecting generated keywords to actions that occur either during parsing or during execution.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical disclosure paragraph for a programming language extension framework where schemas are converted into keywords and parsed into function calls.
counterfactuals.output: A programming language extension framework is disclosed in which declarative schemas are used to define new language constructs without modifying the core compiler or interpreter. Each schema specifies a keyword, expected argument structure, type constraints, optional parameters, and an associated semantic action. During initialization, the framework registers the schema-defined keywords with a parser extension layer. When source code containing one of the registered keywords is encountered, the parser validates the syntax against the corresponding schema and transforms the matched construct into an intermediate function-call representation. The generated function call includes the parsed arguments, metadata derived from the schema, and any contextual information required for execution or compilation. The resulting representation may then be passed to an existing runtime, compiler backend, macro system, or code-generation pipeline, thereby allowing domain-specific language features to be introduced through schema definitions while preserving compatibility with the host language’s standard execution model.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an abstract in patent language for a system that introduces schematized data object syntax into an existing programming language using schema processor and document generator modules.
counterfactuals.output: An apparatus, system, and computer-implemented method are provided for introducing schematized data object syntax into an existing programming language. A schema processor module receives one or more schema definitions defining structural, semantic, and type constraints for data objects expressible within source code of the programming language. The schema processor module parses the schema definitions and generates corresponding language-integrated object representations, validation rules, access interfaces, and/or compilation artifacts configured to interoperate with native constructs of the programming language. A document generator module processes the schema definitions and/or generated artifacts to produce documentation identifying permissible object syntax, object hierarchies, field definitions, data types, constraints, and usage conventions. The system thereby enables developers to declare, instantiate, manipulate, validate, and document schematized data objects using syntax integrated with the existing programming language, without requiring a separate external data description language or manual translation layer. counterfactuals.prompt: Describe, in formal patent terminology, a method for defining custom language keywords with parse-time and runtime actions based on metadata and schema representations.
counterfactuals.output:
A computer-implemented method is provided for defining custom language keywords having associated parse-time and runtime behavior, the method comprising receiving, by one or more processors, a keyword definition comprising metadata identifying a keyword token, at least one syntactic constraint, and at least one semantic attribute associated with the keyword. The method further comprises generating, from the keyword definition, a schema representation specifying a structural form of a language construct corresponding to the keyword, the schema representation including one or more permitted child elements, operand types, attribute fields, validation rules, or execution parameters.

The method further comprises registering the keyword definition and the schema representation in a keyword registry accessible to a parser. During parsing of a source document or program text, the parser detects an occurrence of the keyword token and retrieves the corresponding metadata and schema representation from the keyword registry. The parser then validates the detected occurrence against the schema representation, including verifying conformance of one or more arguments, operands, nested statements, annotations, or contextual placement conditions. In response to successful validation, the parser generates an intermediate representation node corresponding to the custom keyword, the intermediate representation node including metadata-derived properties and schema-derived structural information.

The method further comprises associating a parse-time action with the keyword definition, the parse-time action being executable during parsing, validation, transformation, or compilation of the source document. The parse-time action may include modifying a parse tree, expanding the keyword into one or more lower-level constructs, enforcing a compile-time constraint, resolving a symbol, generating diagnostic information, or annotating the intermediate representation node.

The method further comprises associating a runtime action with the keyword definition, the runtime action being executable during interpretation, execution, or evaluation of the intermediate representation. The runtime action may include invoking a handler function, performing a state transition, evaluating an expression, binding a resource, dispatching an event, executing generated code, or applying behavior specified by the metadata.

In certain embodiments, the metadata includes one or more of a keyword identifier, version identifier, namespace, precedence value, associativity rule, arity specification, type signature, permission requirement, documentation field, default value, lifecycle hook, or execution policy. In certain embodiments, the schema representation is expressed as a structured data model, including JSON Schema, XML Schema, protocol buffer definitions, abstract syntax tree descriptors, grammar fragments, or a domain-specific schema language.

In operation, the method enables extension of a programming language, scripting language, configuration language, markup language, or domain-specific language without requiring modification of a core parser implementation. A keyword provider may define the keyword by supplying metadata, schema constraints, and one or more action handlers. The parser and runtime environment may dynamically load the keyword definition, validate usage of the custom keyword at parse time, and execute the associated runtime action when the corresponding intermediate representation node is encountered.

In one embodiment, the method further comprises serializing the keyword definition into a portable package including the metadata, schema representation, parse-time action reference, and runtime action reference. The portable package may be distributed to a plurality of execution environments, each of which may register the custom keyword and enforce the schema-defined syntax and metadata-defined behavior. In another embodiment, the method further comprises enforcing compatibility by comparing a version field of the keyword definition with a runtime capability descriptor before enabling execution of the runtime action.

Accordingly, the method provides a metadata-driven and schema-driven mechanism for defining extensible custom language keywords, wherein parse-time validation and transformation and runtime execution behavior are specified declaratively or semi-declaratively and are bound to the keyword through a registry-accessible definition.
